topics.title: What cloud computing is

kcs.statement: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.

On premises, an organisation buys, houses and maintains its own servers in its own data center; in the cloud, the provider owns and runs the hardware and the customer rents capacity only when it needs it.

serves.reason: Exam questions in Domain 1 assume the AWS definition of cloud computing and test it directly against on-premises wording.

problem_ideas: A startup needs 20 servers for a 3-day product launch: compare buying them with renting them in the cloud.
Pick the option that matches the AWS definition of cloud computing from four near-miss definitions (one omits pay-as-you-go, one omits the internet).
A hospital runs its own server room: list three tasks it stops doing if it moves the workload to AWS.
Classify six statements as describing on-premises IT or cloud computing.
A team waited 6 weeks for a server purchase order; explain what on-demand delivery changes.
Spot the wrong claim: 'In the cloud you still buy the hardware, AWS just hosts it.'

topics.title: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS: who manages what

kcs.statement: IaaS provides virtual servers, storage and networking; the customer manages the operating system, runtime, application and data, as with Amazon EC2.
PaaS runs the underlying infrastructure and operating system for you, so the customer only deploys and manages the application and its data, as with AWS Elastic Beanstalk.
SaaS delivers a complete application operated by the provider; the customer only uses it and manages their own data and user access, as with web email or a hosted CRM.

serves.reason: The exam asks which service model fits a stated level of control, and this split also underlies the shared responsibility questions.

requires.reason: Service models are defined as ways of consuming cloud computing.

problem_ideas: A team wants full control over OS patches and custom kernel settings: pick IaaS, PaaS or SaaS.
A developer only wants to upload code and not manage servers: name the model and an AWS example.
Sort EC2, Elastic Beanstalk and a hosted email product into IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Fill in a responsibility table (hardware, OS, runtime, app, data) for each of the three models.
An accounting firm buys a ready-made payroll web app: which model is it, and what does the firm still manage?
Spot the distractor: 'With SaaS the customer patches the application servers.'

topics.title: Cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployment

kcs.statement: In a cloud (all-in) deployment, every part of the application runs in the cloud, whether it was built there or migrated from on premises.
A hybrid deployment connects cloud resources to on-premises infrastructure, for example keeping a legacy system in the company data center while new features run in AWS.

An on-premises deployment, also called a private cloud, uses virtualisation and resource management tools in the organisation's own data center; it gives full control but not the cost benefits of the public cloud.

serves.reason: Task statement 3.1 asks the learner to identify cloud, hybrid and on-premises deployment models from a scenario.

requires.reason: Deployment models contrast cloud computing with on-premises data centers.

problem_ideas: A bank must keep its mainframe on site but wants to run a new mobile app in AWS: name the deployment model.
A new startup builds everything in AWS from day one: which deployment model is this?

topics.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling

kcs.statement: Vertical scaling (scaling up) makes a single server bigger, with more CPU or memory; it is limited by the largest available machine and is common for non-distributed systems such as a database.
Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more servers that share the load; it needs a distributed application and is how web tiers usually scale in the cloud.

problem_ideas: A database server hits 95% memory: does moving from 16 GB to 64 GB RAM scale up or out?
A web shop goes from 2 to 10 identical web servers for Black Friday: name the scaling direction.
Which approach hits a hard ceiling, and why?

A legacy app keeps session state on one machine: which scaling type is easiest and why?
Order three changes (bigger instance, more instances, add a load balancer) by which ones need a distributed app.

topics.title: Elasticity and agility

kcs.statement: Elasticity is automatically adding and removing resources as demand changes, so a workload pays only for the capacity it needs at that moment.
Scalability is the ability to handle more load by adding resources; elasticity adds automation in both directions, scaling out when demand rises and back in when it falls.
In AWS terms, agility is how fast new IT resources become available (minutes instead of weeks), which lowers the cost and time of experimenting and innovating.

serves.reason: Choosing the cloud benefit that fits a scenario means telling elasticity, scalability and agility apart.
Task statement 1.1 names elasticity and agility explicitly.

requires.reason: Elasticity is defined as automated scaling, so scaling out and in must be known first.

problem_ideas: A ticket site's traffic jumps 10x for 2 hours then drops: which benefit lets it avoid paying for peak all day?

topics.title: High availability: surviving a failure

kcs.statement: High availability means designing a workload to minimise downtime so it keeps meeting its availability target when components fail; a common technique is running redundant copies in independent locations, which in AWS means multiple Availability Zones.

Redundancy only gives high availability when traffic fails over automatically, the data is available in the surviving location and the remaining capacity can carry the load; horizontal scaling within one location adds capacity for more load but does not by itself make a workload highly available.

serves.reason: Scenario questions ask whether a benefit is high availability or elasticity, and that choice feeds the reliability pillar.
Task statement 1.1 lists high availability as a benefit to recognise.

requires.reason: The second KC contrasts high availability with horizontal scaling, so scaling out must be known first.

problem_ideas: An app runs on 4 servers in one data center that loses power: is it highly available? What change fixes it?

topics.title: Fixed vs variable costs: CapEx and OpEx

kcs.statement: Fixed costs, such as buying servers and data center space up front, are paid whether or not the capacity is used; this up-front spending is capital expenditure (CapEx).
Variable costs rise and fall with actual usage; in the cloud, spending becomes operational expenditure (OpEx) for only the resources consumed.
With fixed on-premises capacity, an organisation must size for forecast peak demand, so capacity sits idle most of the time or runs out when demand beats the forecast.

serves.reason: 'Trade fixed expense for variable expense' is the benefit learners most often need to identify.
Task statement 1.4 asks for the role of fixed versus variable costs.

problem_ideas: A company buys 10 servers at $6,000 each for a peak it reaches 1 month a year: compute the yearly idle capacity in server-months.

topics.title: Total cost of ownership and hidden on-prem costs

kcs.statement: Total cost of ownership (TCO) counts every cost of running a workload over its life, not just hardware: facilities, power, cooling, networking, software licences and staff time.
On-premises costs that are often left out of comparisons include data center space, power and cooling, physical security, hardware refresh cycles and the people who rack, patch and repair servers.
Moving to the cloud lowers TCO mainly by removing data center overhead and idle capacity, and by freeing staff from undifferentiated heavy lifting to work that serves customers.

serves.reason: Task statement 1.4 covers costs associated with on-premises environments and the savings of moving to the cloud.

requires.reason: TCO comparisons are built from fixed on-premises costs against variable cloud costs.

problem_ideas: A comparison lists only $200k of server hardware: name four missing on-premises cost lines.

topics.title: Economies of scale and the value of automation

kcs.statement: Because AWS pools usage from hundreds of thousands of customers, it buys and runs hardware more cheaply than one company could, and passes the savings on as lower pay-as-you-go prices.
Automating provisioning and operations makes deployments repeatable and consistent, reduces human error, and cuts the staff time and cost of running workloads compared with one-time manual steps.

serves.reason: Task statement 1.4 names economies of scale and the benefits of automation.

topics.title: Rightsizing: pay for what you actually use

kcs.statement: Rightsizing is matching instance types and sizes to a workload's measured performance and capacity needs at the lowest cost, for example moving a server that averages 10% CPU to a smaller size.
Rightsizing is an ongoing process based on utilisation data, and it should happen before committing to long-term discounts, because the cloud lets you change size at any time.

serves.reason: Task statement 1.4 asks for the concept of rightsizing, and it recurs in billing questions.

topics.title: The AWS value proposition: six advantages

kcs.statement: AWS names six advantages of cloud computing: trade fixed expense for variable expense, benefit from massive economies of scale, stop guessing capacity, increase speed and agility, stop spending money running and maintaining data centers, and go global in minutes.
'Stop guessing capacity' means using only as much capacity as demand needs and scaling as it changes, instead of buying for a forecast that leaves resources idle or short.
'Go global in minutes' means deploying an application to AWS locations around the world in a few clicks, giving distant users lower latency at little extra cost.

serves.reason: Picking the cloud benefit that fits a scenario uses exactly these six named advantages.
Task statement 1.1 covers the value proposition and the benefits of global reach.

requires.reason: The first advantage is stated as fixed versus variable expense.

topics.title: Well-Architected Framework and cloud design principles

kcs.statement: The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a set of best practices and review questions for evaluating a cloud architecture across six pillars; it guides design reviews and does not deploy or change resources.

Core AWS design principles include designing for failure by removing every single point of failure, decoupling components so one failing part does not break the rest, and using elasticity instead of fixed capacity.
AWS design principles treat servers as disposable resources and favour automation: replace a faulty server with a fresh one built automatically instead of repairing it by hand.

serves.reason: A learner cannot pick a pillar for a scenario without knowing what the framework is and its guiding principles.
Task statement 1.2 covers the Well-Architected Framework and design principles.

requires.reason: Designing for failure is stated in terms of removing single points of failure.
One design principle is to use elasticity instead of fixed capacity.

topics.title: Pillars I: operational excellence, security, reliability

kcs.statement: The six Well-Architected pillars are operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability.

The operational excellence pillar covers running and monitoring systems and improving processes: perform operations as code, make frequent small reversible changes, and learn from operational failures.
The security pillar protects data, systems and assets through a strong identity foundation, traceability, security at all layers, and protecting data in transit and at rest.
The reliability pillar makes a workload recover from failure and meet demand: automatically recover from failure, test recovery procedures, scale horizontally and stop guessing capacity.

serves.reason: The outcome asks the learner to pick the right pillar for a scenario, which needs these three pillars' principles.
Task statement 1.2 asks for the differences between the pillars.

requires.reason: Pillars are the structure of the framework, so the framework must be known first.

problem_ideas: 'Test your recovery procedures': which pillar? Reliability versus operational excellence is the trap.

topics.title: Pillars II: performance, cost, sustainability

kcs.statement: The performance efficiency pillar is about using computing resources efficiently as demand and technology change: democratise advanced technologies, go global in minutes, use serverless architectures and experiment more often.

The cost optimization pillar delivers business value at the lowest price: adopt a consumption model, measure overall efficiency, stop spending on undifferentiated heavy lifting, and analyse and attribute expenditure.
The sustainability pillar, added in 2021, minimises a workload's environmental impact: maximise utilisation, use managed services and adopt more efficient hardware and software.
Removing idle or oversized resources to cut spending maps to cost optimization, while choosing faster resource types or adding caching to cut latency maps to performance efficiency.

serves.reason: Choosing the right pillar for a scenario needs these three pillars, especially the cost versus performance split.
Task statement 1.2 asks for the differences between the pillars.

requires.reason: Each pillar is a part of the Well-Architected Framework, so the framework and its purpose must be known first.

topics.title: AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF)

kcs.statement: The AWS Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) organises guidance for a cloud transformation into six perspectives, helping an organisation find gaps in skills and processes before and during adoption.
The CAF's business-focused perspectives are Business, People and Governance; its technical perspectives are Platform, Security and Operations.
AWS lists four business outcomes of using the CAF: reduced business risk, improved environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance, increased revenue and increased operational efficiency.
The CAF's transformation domains are Technology, Process, Organization and Product, and the adoption journey runs through four phases: Envision, Align, Launch and Scale.

serves.reason: The outcome asks the learner to pick the CAF perspective for a scenario.

topics.title: Migration strategies: the 7 Rs

kcs.statement: The seven migration strategies (the 7 Rs) are retire, retain, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform and refactor (re-architect).

Rehost ('lift and shift') moves an application as-is, while replatform ('lift, tinker and shift') adds a few cloud optimisations, such as moving a database to a managed service, without changing the core architecture.
Refactor re-architects an application with cloud-native features to gain scale, agility or performance and takes the most effort, while repurchase replaces it with a different product, usually SaaS.

Retire switches off applications that are no longer needed, retain keeps applications on premises for now, and relocate moves virtualised infrastructure (for example VMware) to the cloud without buying hardware or changing the applications.

serves.reason: The outcome asks the learner to pick the migration strategy (7 Rs) for a scenario.
Task statement 1.3 asks for appropriate migration strategies.

requires.reason: Repurchase is defined as moving to SaaS.
Retain and relocate are described relative to on-premises deployment.
